title: Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips
comment: Extended version of the paper titled "Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips'' to appear in MICRO 2026
summary:
We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips. Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data-pattern-dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips. Out of our 13 new findings and 6 key takeaway messages, we highlight: 1) a read operation consumes significantly higher current than any other operation and 2) the toggled data bus signals in a data transfer burst significantly affect current draw where toggling all HBM2-internal bank group bus signals causes 29.4% higher power consumption than keeping them constant. Leveraging our empirical insights into HBM2 power consumption, we engineer an access pattern that yields 23.6% higher power consumption on average across 36 tested HBM2 chips than the highest-power-consuming JEDEC-specified current measurement loop.
  Our results have important implications for HBM-based system design and validation. Relying solely on JEDEC- or vendor-specified test loops to bound HBM power could cause system failures and/or thermal throttling in real-world high-power AI/ML workloads. To improve 3D-stacked DRAM power modeling in open source architectural simulation infrastructures, we develop a new HBM power model. Our model predicts the power of 36 real HBM2 chips across diverse workloads (including a real LLM decode workload) with 7.6 -- 8.1% mean absolute percentage error, substantially more accurately than state-of-the-art HBM power models. The power consumption predicted by our model for a power-intensive microbenchmark closely matches (with 2.4% to 5.3% error across HBM3E's specified supply voltage range) the average HBM3E memory power consumed by three tested NVIDIA H200 GPUs. We publicly release our power model at https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/HBM-Power.

title: DFIT: A Framework for Building Instrumentation Tools Across Heterogeneous Dataflow Accelerators
comment: Accepted at the 22nd European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys '27), April 19-23, 2027, Rabat, Morocco. 14 pages, 8 figures
summary:
Emerging dataflow accelerators offer exceptional energy efficiency and throughput for machine learning workloads, yet remain largely opaque to developers for performance analysis. Unlike CPUs and GPUs, where instrumentation frameworks enable fine-grained introspection, dataflow hardware exposes little information. This lack of transparency limits the ability of compiler engineers, system designers, and application developers to analyze, tune, or debug accelerator behavior.
  In this paper, we introduce DFIT (DataFlow Accelerator Instrumentation Tool), an instrumentation framework designed specifically for dataflow architectures. DFIT directly instruments operations, regions, and compiler transformations at the graph IR and backend-lowering stages using semantic program representation. DFIT captures high-level, semantically meaningful data that reflect the true dataflow of computation. These data can be exported for visualization and analysis. Our approach demonstrates how instrumentation can be generalized beyond traditional hardware to support heterogeneous architectures, providing portability without modifying tool logic.
  By opening the black box of dataflow execution, DFIT establishes a foundation for new classes of performance analysis tools for AI accelerators. It provides a practical path toward reproducible, architecture-aware introspection across heterogeneous systems, bridging the long-standing visibility gap between compiler design, runtime scheduling, and hardware realization. Evaluation across Cerebras, SambaNova, and TPU shows practical overhead of 3.53%-13.62% across instrumentation modes with robust cross-platform portability.

title: HADES: A Programmable Processing-Near-Memory Engine for Binary Similarity Search
summary: Moving operands to a processor can cost more than the arithmetic performed on them, and for small binary similarity and search workloads data movement can dominate. We present HADES, a programmable processing-near-memory engine built around one shared 32x32-bit 2R1W register-file macro that holds both data and program. Twelve 16-bit opcodes, three working registers and a 32-slot program express ten search workloads in 8 to 19 slots, and SCANP and SCANSEL shorten dual-row and selected scans. A post-layout 2x2 Tiny Tapeout implementation closes timing at 40 MHz with 26,968 square microns of standard cells beside a 15,744 square microns macro. All HADES results come from RTL or gate-level simulation of this implementation, and HADES energy is estimated. Against ESP8266 and ESP32 microcontrollers running plain C, and with an ideal host, HADES answers a resident query 10x to 32x and 2.2x to 11x faster, respectively. End to end, it wins at the evaluated batch sizes of B = 16 and B = 256 against both boards and loses the single-query (B = 1) runs to the ESP32. An Arduino Nano runs a restricted subset. Kernel power stays within about 2% of a spin loop on all three boards. These results hold for plain-C baselines under the evaluated conditions. At this scale the control and instruction storage fit around a shared memory macro, while the byte-wide interface and the loading path remain significant costs.

title: "Is Low Power Enough?" Rethinking Energy Efficiency in High-Fidelity Sensing
summary: For two decades, long-lived sensor nodes have been built from the lowest-power parts, because their scalar readings take only milliseconds to acquire and send. Scientists now want higher fidelity data from the field, such as images and audio, and these observations break that rule: a low-power microcontroller stays awake for seconds to read, store, and transmit each one, so low power is no longer low energy. We argue that long-lived, high-fidelity nodes should instead be built around a more capable microcontroller, provided the whole board sleeps deeply. We revisit two principles from early sensor networks, "race to sleep" and "talk less", for high-fidelity data and on-device AI, and test them by comparing the STM32N6, which pairs a fast core with a neural accelerator, against the low-power Apollo4 Plus. Although the STM32N6 draws 1.9x more power, it completes an observation (capture, storage, on-board detection, and a LoRa transmission) 9.9x faster and so uses 5.2x less energy. On the same model, it runs inference with 3.2-11.4x less energy, and it fits models over 23 points more accurate. A high-fidelity node lives longest when it finishes quickly, sleeps deeply, and sends only what matters.

title: Learning to Sync at the Edge: Client-Side Adaptive Synchronization for Federated Learning
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables. Accepted to IEEE SEC 2026
summary: The scalability and performance of edge federated learning are fundamentally constrained by synchronization bottlenecks. Clients operate under heterogeneous compute, time-varying communication conditions, and, in some settings, privacy constraints, yet synchronization is often still handled with fixed schedules. However, synchronization decisions are often made outside the client, even though the client directly observes local progress, resource state, and communication conditions. We present a client-side reinforcement learning synchronization framework in which each client decides during training whether to upload, download, synchronize bidirectionally, or defer communication. The framework places a lightweight scheduler alongside the local model and formulates synchronization as a resource-aware control problem driven by local learning and system state. We study this framework on two representative edge workloads, spatiotemporal traffic forecasting and image classification. Across both settings, adaptive client-side synchronization improves the accuracy-cost trade-off, reducing system cost in traffic forecasting while maintaining competitive cost and improving final accuracy in image classification. We also consider privacy-constrained settings, where synchronization must account for not only latency and energy but also privacy expenditure. Overall, our results show that synchronization in edge federated learning is better treated as an adaptive client-side control problem than only as a server-side coordination mechanism.

title: Lava: Foundations for Liquid Haskell via Translation to Rocq
summary:
Liquid Haskell is an extension of the Glasgow Haskell compiler (GHC) that adds support for refinement types: types restricted by logical predicates. Specifications are automatically checked by an SMT solver, thus offering lightweight verification directly within the language. However, the necessarily large trusted codebase behind Liquid Haskell (from GHC to the SMT solver to the refinement typechecker itself) raises the question of trust in the verification and the necessity for a formalized semantics of Liquid Haskell linked to its implementation. Grounding Liquid Haskell in theory is complicated by the interaction between two semantic levels in the language: a computational one and a logical one (for refinement predicates). While both are well understood separately, their interaction is subtle and has only been partially described.
  We give a semantics to Liquid Haskell by translation to Rocq. Both the computational and logical parts are translated to the same language, with a well-understood semantics; our translation makes the discrepancy between the two semantic levels explicit. The translation is implemented in Haskell and comes with a Rocq library that includes powerful proof automation standing in for the SMT solver. Thus, on the practical level, our tool Lava serves as a certificate checker for the supported subset of Liquid Haskell.

title: Grover Search for a Threshold-Fraction Variant of the Travelling Salesman Problem: A Circuit-Level Construction
summary: The Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) is a classic combinatorial optimisation problem which is NP-hard in optimisation form and NP-complete as a decision problem. The standard question asks for the shortest tour that visits every city exactly once and returns to the origin. This paper studies a threshold-fraction variant, which we call the robust TSP, formulated as a promise problem: given a distance threshold $K$ and a promised fraction $p$, decide whether at least a fraction $p$ of all tours have total length at most $K$, or whether no such tour exists. We show that Grover's quantum search algorithm decides this problem using $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ oracle queries, independent of the number of cities $N$, with each query implemented by a quantum circuit of polynomial size in $N$. For any fixed robustness level $p$, the total runtime is therefore polynomial in $N$. Measured in oracle queries, the quantum algorithm offers a quadratic improvement in the dependence on $1/p$ over classical random sampling, which needs $Θ(1/p)$ samples; because each quantum query is costly, however, it is faster in total running time only when $p$ is very small (roughly below $N^{-4}$), where the number of queries is no longer constant. We describe the problem formulation, detail the oracle construction (edge-length loading, sequential quantum addition, and threshold comparison), and analyse the query complexity to achieve the required result.

title: GaborFlow: Hardware-Software Co-Optimization of Gabor Filter Accelerator Design
summary: Brain tumor classification from MRI scans represents a critical challenge in medical imaging, where accuracy directly impacts patient outcomes. This paper introduces GaborFlow, a novel hardware-software co-optimization framework that revolutionizes the design of the Gabor Filter accelerator for generating feature maps to enhance brain tumor detection. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on fixed filter parameters, our method employs trainable Gabor coefficients within a carefully optimized range, integrated with an EfficientNet-B0 backbone CNN architecture. The innovation lies in the synergistic combination of software optimization through Bayesian hyperparameter tuning and hardware efficiency through precision-optimized multipliers. Our GF baseline accelerator achieves remarkable results, with 98.6% classification accuracy, 28.08% power benefits, and 48.83% footprint savings compared to state-of-the-art implementations, demonstrating that medical AI can be both highly accurate and energy-efficient. The hardware design files are made freely available for easy adoption and further usage by the researchers and designers.

title: Byzantine-linearizable Single-Writer Multi-Reader Register in the GPU-Inspired Shared Memory Model
summary: The construction of fault-tolerant atomic registers is a fundamental problem in distributed computing. GPUs, widely used in scientific computing and machine learning, face Byzantine thread behaviour, while their shared memory lacks access control, allowing any thread to modify shared objects. This raises the question of whether atomic register semantics can be maintained when any thread, including the designated writer, may behave Byzantine. We study this problem in the GPU-inspired shared-memory model of Georgiou et al. and present implementations of a Byzantine-linearizable single-writer multi-reader (SWMR) register. CAReg uses constant memory with a quantifiable probability of invalid reads, while SnapObject maintains a bounded window of authenticated writes, eliminating invalid reads and tolerating up to \(n-1\) Byzantine processes through lock-free and wait-free variants. Our results demonstrate how GPU phase-based, lock-step execution can partially compensate for the absence of access control.

title: (Implicitly) Characterizing Probabilistic Polynomial Time as Used in Cryptography
comment: Extended version of a paper to appear in the proceedings of FSTTCS 2026
summary: In this paper, we show how a recently introduced $λ$-calculus for randomized computation, called $λ\mathbf{BLL}$, can accurately capture the notions of first- and second-order polytime computations used in cryptographic definitions and proofs. These results, spelled out in the style of so-called \emph{implicit computational complexity}, imply that $λ\mathbf{BLL}$ is sufficiently powerful to express experiments and adversaries as used in cryptography, and that reductions, when formulated within the calculus, are guaranteed to be complexity-preserving. Remarkably, while polynomial-time soundness holds for the full calculus, polynomial-time completeness already follows in presence of a minimal finite set of basic functions.

title: Many Scores Force Many Reads: An Optimality Proof for Score of Parentheses
summary:
LeetCode Problem 856, Score of Parentheses, admits a one-pass algorithm using $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary registers. Its correctness follows from a local interpretation: every occurrence of () contributes a power of two determined by its nesting depth. The space bound is immediately optimal in the usual programming-challenge model, but the linear-time bound is less obvious. In particular, a direct adversary that forces an algorithm to inspect every character is difficult to maintain under the promise that the input is balanced.
  We instead prove a counting lower bound. For every $k$, we construct $2^k$ balanced parenthesis strings of the same length $4k+2$, all having distinct scores. The construction encodes each bit using one of two operations, changing a current score $v$ to either $2v+1$ or $2v+2$. Consequently, any deterministic character-query decision tree computing the score must have depth at least $k$. A two-character padding argument extends the result to every even input length, proving an $Ω(n)$ worst-case time lower bound. The one-pass algorithm is therefore asymptotically optimal in the unit-cost RAM model.

title: Programmable Data Layouts via On-The-Fly Data Transformation
summary: The performance of modern computing systems is heavily bottlenecked by the widening gap between processing throughput and main memory latency, a problem exacerbated when an application's logical data access patterns misalign with the physical layout of data in memory. To address this, we propose a hardware-software co-design framework comprising the Data Transformation Language (DTL) and the Data Transformation Unit (DTU). DTL allows programmers to concisely express complex data layout reorganizations, which the compiler translates into efficient hardware routing configurations. The DTU, a hardware engine logically situated between the Last-Level Cache (LLC) and main memory, transparently evaluates these configurations on-the-fly to gather scattered data elements into dense, logically contiguous cache lines. By converting explicit layout transformations into virtual views, this approach eliminates the need for explicit data materialization in software. We evaluate the DTU within a quad-core RISC-V SoC using FireSim, demonstrating substantial improvements in execution speed and memory efficiency.

title: A Self-Defining Operator for Distributed Applications
summary: To operate distributed applications with high availability, operators must rapidly diagnose and mitigate any incident. LLM-based agents can help, but unlike experienced human operators they do not improve as they handle more incidents. Each investigation starts from scratch, re-deriving likely causes and re-testing hypotheses even when a similar fault was resolved in the past. We present a self-defining operator (SDO) that improves with time by updating its operational behavior and memory. When SDO resolves an incident, it distills that experience into playbooks, which describe reusable diagnostic instructions for future incidents with similar faults, and detectors, scripts that take application telemetry as input and output relevant playbook(s). SDO continuously runs the detectors and invokes LLMs only when one fires, so its token cost scales with incident count rather than with operational time. Across 11 open-source microservice applications, SDO cuts resolution time by 52% on recurring faults while keeping per-incident cost low. SDO is open source at https://github.com/uw-syfi/sdo.

title: Mechanising Denotational Semantics in Agda
comment: 23 pages, excl. references. To be published in Proceedings of MFPS 2026
summary:
Mechanisation of a mathematical definition (also referred to as formalisation) has many benefits. Here, we focus on mechanising denotational semantic definitions of programming languages by embedding them in the Agda language. The Agda type-checker detects and reports any issues with the wellformedness and type correctness of the embedded definitions.
  To minimise the effort required, and to facilitate correlation of the original definition with its Agda embedding, mechanisation should not involve significant reformulation or extension. Here, we show how to embed conventional Scott-Strachey denotational definitions in Agda with almost no changes to $λ$-notation or domain equations.
  Agda notation for definitions of types and functions corresponds closely to the conventional meta-notation of denotational semantics. We have developed a collection of Agda modules with postulated types for commonly used domain constructors and their associated operations.
  We illustrate our approach with mechanisations of three denotational definitions: a model of the untyped $λ$-calculus, Plotkin's denotational semantics of PCF, and a semantics of a sublanguage of Scheme. In previous work, similar mechanisations in Agda have revealed several unsuspected wellformedness issues in published denotational definitions.
  Some of the postulated properties of our definitions are inconsistent with a classical set-theoretic interpretation of Agda. We conjecture that they would be consistent with an interpretation of Agda in a higher-order intuititionistic logic, such as that used by Simpson in his work on synthetic domain theory. After recalling previous work on mechanising domain theory, we consider the possibility of mechanising synthetic domain theory in Agda.

title: Faster Deterministic Approximation for Counting Knapsack
summary:
Given $n$ nonnegative integer weights $w_1, \ldots, w_n$ and an integer knapsack capacity $T$, the $\#$Knapsack problem asks to count the number of subsets $I \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ such that $\sum_{i \in I} w_i \le T$. A long line of research has been devoted to designing faster $(1 \pm \varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for this \#P-hard problem. Until very recently, the best-known time complexity was $\tilde{O}\bigl(n^{2.5}/\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)\bigr)$, achieved by the randomized algorithm of [Dyer, STOC 2003] and the deterministic algorithm of [Gawrychowski, Markin, and Weimann, ICALP 2018]. The recent work by [Feng and Jin, SODA 2025] improved the randomized complexity to $\tilde{O}\bigl(n^{1.5}/\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)\bigr)$, leaving open the question whether this $n^{2.5}$ barrier could also be broken by a \emph{deterministic} algorithm.
  In this work, we answer this question in the affirmative by presenting a deterministic $(1 + \varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for \#Knapsack in $\tilde{O}\bigl(n^{2.4}/\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)\bigr)$ time. Our key technical innovation is to deterministically simulate the balancing technique, which was previously used in the literature of knapsack-type problems via random partitions and seemed to require randomization.

title: MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning
summary: Efficient task scheduling in heterogeneous computing systems remains a fundamental challenge in embedded and high-level synthesis flows. This paper presents MoSAIC (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition), a learning-based framework that bridges the gap between exact and heuristic scheduling approaches for DAG-based applications. The system uses the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to learn the relationships between DAG structures and scheduling priority functions. The framework first leverages the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver [4] to generate optimal schedules, which are then used to supervise the learning of compact priority-based scheduling functions through Bayesian Optimization. These learned heuristics capture relationships between scheduling decisions and structural graph features such as rank, depth, and fanout, enabling the construction of a reusable knowledge base across diverse DAG instances. Experimental results across synthetic graph families and real-world benchmarks, including PolyBench and MachSuite, show that the learned heuristics consistently improve over classical approaches such as HEFT [2], while maintaining low runtime overhead. The results indicate that combining optimal supervision with learning-based generalization provides a practical approach for scalable and adaptive task scheduling.

title: Dissecting the Carbon-SLO Tension in Geo-Distributed LLM Serving
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) inference is driving a growing share of datacenter carbon emissions. Although carbon-aware scheduling can reduce these emissions in geo-distributed datacenters by exploiting the spatiotemporal variations in grid carbon intensity, the latency-sensitive nature of LLM serving constrains this design space. While prior studies investigate the carbon savings achievable through spatial scheduling, they oversimplify the dynamics of modern inference engines, such as queueing and continuous batching, which strongly shape inference latency. We address this issue by designing and evaluating a latency-centric, geo-distributed inference simulator, calibrated with hardware-grounded latency and power measurements, that reproduces these dynamics and enables the study of carbon savings under strict service-level objectives (SLOs). We then formulate a series of SLO- and carbon-aware schedulers of increasing sophistication, from per-request heuristics to batch-level optimization: (i) a greedy heuristic, (ii) an integer linear programming (ILP)-based scheduler jointly assigning batches of requests, (iii) an iterative ILP-based solution projecting its own assignments back into the load estimates to capture load coupling, and (iv) a facility mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler pricing the energy of batched requests collectively rather than in isolation. Across three LLMs under MLPerf SLOs and varying system loads, the MILP-based option offers the best carbon-SLO balance, reducing carbon emissions by up to 60% relative to the round-robin policy, with an average SLO violation of 3%. Our characterization further shows that savings grow with the spread of carbon intensity across datacenters and shrink as system load increases, while SLO attainment depends on how frequently schedulers receive datacenters' load updates.

title: Contravariant Universe Subtyping, Formalized, Mechanized
summary:
In a type theory with a cumulative universe hierarchy, \emph{subtyping} is often incorporated to lift lower universe levels to higher ones. In practice, kernels of proof assistants typically implement universe subtyping conservatively: subtyping only propagates covariantly into the output types of $Π$ types, while input types must be equivalent. A full-blown subtyping relation also compares the input types contravariantly. However, contravariant subtyping is not justified by the existing set-theoretic model, and poses challenges in the development of a complete subtyping algorithm.
  We present \mclttsub, a complete mechanized study of contravariant universe subtyping for a core Martin-Löf type theory (MLTT), built as an extension of the verified McTT kernel in Rocq. We re-establish the syntactic meta-theory and the soundness and completeness properties of the normalization-by-evaluation (NbE) algorithm. To complete the verified pipeline for a type-checker, we give two complete and sound subtyping algorithms. The first one \emph{renormalizes} output types in every $Π$ iteration. Despite a simple completeness proof, this algorithm incurs additional computational cost. The second algorithm hence circumvents this cost by avoiding the renormalization at all. It simply recursively compares two already normalized types structurally. Nevertheless, a completeness proof of this algorithm in a semantic approach requires to reason about normalization in sub-contexts, a capability beyond what the current semantic gadget offers. Instead, we conduct a program equivalence proof through bisimulation relations. Using this technique, we prove that the NbE algorithm returns equal normal forms in sub-contexts up to universe levels, and successfully conclude the completeness of the subtyping algorithm.

title: The Matching Number Characterizes the Query Complexity of Edge Counting and Degree Moment Estimation
summary: Consider an unknown graph $G = (V,E)$ with vertex degrees $d_v$, accessed only by sampling uniformly random edges and querying the degrees of their endpoints. We study the query complexity of estimating the number of edges $m$ and the degree moments $M_s = \sum_{v \in V} (d_v)^s$ for fixed integers $s \ge 2$. In this model, [Beretta and Tětek, TALG 2024] estimate $m$ within relative error $\varepsilon$ using $O(\log n/\varepsilon^2+\sqrt n/\varepsilon)$ expected queries without knowing the number of vertices $n$, and [Bhattacharya and Pradhan, CIAC 2025] estimate $M_s$ using $O(n^{1-1/s}/\varepsilon^2)$ queries when $n$ is given. We show that the query complexity of both problems is governed by the matching number $ν$ of $G$ (the maximum number of pairwise disjoint edges) rather than the number of vertices $n$, and that the dependence on $\varepsilon$ for degree moments can be polynomially improved. Our algorithms rest on a simple observation: the endpoints of a maximum matching cover every edge, so a random endpoint of a random edge falls on this set of $2ν$ vertices with probability at least $1/2$. For every $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$, we give advice-free algorithms that estimate $m$ and $M_s$ within relative error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $2/3$, without knowledge of $n$, $ν$, or other graph parameters. Specifically, our algorithms use $O(\min\{ν/\varepsilon, 1/\varepsilon^2+\sqrtν/\varepsilon\})$ expected queries for $m$ and $O(\min\{ν^{1-1/s}/\varepsilon^{2/s}, ν^{1-1/(2s-1)}/\varepsilon^{2/(2s-1)}\})$ for $M_s$. Finally, our lower bounds show that for every $k \ge 2$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, these query complexities are optimal up to constant factors over graphs with matching number at most $k$.

title: The Era of Vibe Tapeout: Dark Age or Golden Age for Analog Circuit Design?
summary: LLM agents now write their own schematic and layout generators, run EDA tools, read the results, and fix the design. This "vibe tapeout" is becoming practical for analog circuits as well. This paper measures how far it has come in two settings. (A) On an open PDK (SKY130), a cloud LLM agent designed an 11-bit, 5.12-MS/s SAR ADC from its specification. The agents produced DRC- and LVS-clean macros and met the specification after parasitic extraction (PEX). In particular, under the condition in which the agent received a sanitized reference design derived from our 65-nm design (vibe porting), it produced the best layout in the shortest time. Its area was 1/1.6 to 1/2.8 of that of the conditions without a reference. This condition reached signoff without human intervention. The agents also identified the causes of post-PEX degradation (CDAC wiring coupling and common-mode-dependent comparator offset) by their own experiments. On the other hand, agents sometimes reported false passes, and verification independent of the design agent was essential. (B) A commercial PDK is under NDA and cannot be given to a cloud LLM. We therefore evaluated local LLMs running on university servers with a six-task benchmark on a commercial 65-nm CMOS PDK. Kimi K3 passed five of the six tasks, while MiniMax M3 passed two. Neither solved the debugging task, which requires finding the cause from symptoms. Finally, we discuss the prospects for extending vibe tapeout from ADCs to entire SoCs, and ask whether vibe tapeout is a dark age or a golden age for analog design. Our answer is that it is a golden age for designers who know what to verify.

title: Vesta: Queueing-Aware LLM Scheduling for Real-World Workloads
summary:
Agentic applications generate multi-turn sequences of LLM requests, with each new turn extending the context accumulated from prior interactions and tool calls. Prefix caching reuses the KV cache of earlier turns and avoids redundant prefill, but routing every turn to its cache-affine instance can create severe local queues while capacity remains idle elsewhere. Remote KV cache access relaxes this tension, yet migrating execution adds transfer work and is harmful when the cluster is already congested. Thus, deciding where to execute a request requires reasoning jointly about cache locality, queueing, and the current operating point of the cluster.
  We present Vesta, a queueing-aware scheduler for distributed agentic LLM serving. Vesta assigns each session a stable holder for its authoritative KV cache while independently selecting an executor for every request. Grounded in classical queueing theory, its objective accounts for backlog, reusable prefixes, KV cache transfer, and the queueing externality of additional service demand; it migrates execution to recover idle capacity when beneficial and favors placements that add the least prefill and transfer work as congestion rises. Vesta also migrates reusable prefixes across length buckets to avoid cold starts. On real-world agentic workloads, Vesta improves throughput by 14.0\% and reduces mean TTFT by 57.8\% over the state-of-the-art scheduler in a PD-colocated deployment. In PD-disaggregated deployments, it reduces mean TTFT by up to 18.1\% and P99 TTFT by up to 29.0\% at matched throughput.

title: Scenario Proofs for Verification of Distributed Protocols
summary: Formal verification of distributed protocols is still dominated by inductive-invariant proofs, whose central challenge is discovering strengthening assertions that rule out unreachable states. This burden is often misaligned with how protocol designers reason: they explain correctness by following representative executions, causal histories, and phase-structured interactions among nodes. This paper introduces scenario proofs, a verification methodology that makes such execution-oriented reasoning formal. A scenario is a structured expression describing representative protocol executions, enriched with ghost variables. Rather than enumerate all possible interleavings, a scenario describes canonical executions and uses a sound semi-commutation relation to account for reorderings that preserve feasibility and final states. Verification then factors into two main obligations. Coverage shows that every feasible protocol execution is equivalent, up to semi-commutation, to one described by the scenario; this obligation is independent of the safety property and serves as a reusable behavioral characterization of the protocol. Correctness proves the desired safety property only over the representative executions, using Hoare-style weakest-precondition reasoning along the scenario structure. We formalize the scenario language, its layered semantics, and proof rules for coverage and correctness. Through case studies of ring leader election, two-phase commit, a decentralized lock, two variants of multi-signature payment, and single-decree Paxos, we show how scenario proofs capture the causal and phase-based arguments used informally by protocol designers. These examples illustrate that scenario proofs can replace monolithic invariant discovery with structured reasoning over representative executions, while retaining a rigorous connection to all feasible protocol behaviors.

title: A Fixed Parameter Sublinear Time Approximation Scheme for Metric Min-Sum Clustering
summary:
Metric $k$-minsum clustering is a simple, natural, appealing density-based clustering criterion whose computational complexity remains poorly understood, despite the progress achieved fornother clustering criteria in the past three decades. In this paper we give an efficient approximation scheme for this problem that runs in sublinear time for mildly increasing $k$, and thus is fixed parameter tractable with respect to the parameter $k$. We complement this result by showing that similar algorithms are unlikely to exist for the closely related problems $k$-median and balanced $k$-median, assuming popular fine-grained complexity conjectures. Specifically, we show that no sublinear time algorithm with small approximation factors can exist even for $2$-median and balanced $2$-median.
  It was previously known that no efficient PTAS can exist for $k$-median and our results show a strong and perhaps surprising separation between the $k$-minsum clustering problem and $k$-median even in the sublinear regime. Our upper bounds improve qualitatively upon decades old results. Our lower bounds establish the first use of the Distributed PCP framework to clustering problems.

title: Stateless Stochastic Computing for Generative AI on Superconducting Logic: A Model-Hardware Co-Design
summary: Thermodynamic computing lets stochastic physical dynamics carry out a computation and reads out the result as a time average. Recently, thermodynamic computing has been demonstrated on several hardware platforms, including digital CMOS circuits based on stochastic computing. Superconducting single-flux-quantum (SFQ) logic offers very high clock rates and very low switching energy, but it heavily penalizes state, memory, fan-out, and feedback, i.e., exactly the per-neuron accumulators on which such designs rely. We therefore realize thermodynamic computing in SFQ logic through a co-design of a generative model and its circuit in which the datapath holds no state at all. The model is a class-conditional flow-matching image generator, which transforms Gaussian noise into an image of the requested class along a short, deterministic path of four Euler steps; in hardware, these steps are unrolled into a feed-forward pipeline of stochastic bitstream operators, whose output is read out as a time average, as in thermodynamic computing, without any relaxation phase. Each layer of the model is a butterfly-factorized linear map built exclusively from multiplexers that operate on split-unipolar bitstreams. The ReLU activation, which in stochastic computing requires a per-neuron up/down counter (accounting for 60-70% of the JJs in a counter-based design), is replaced by a stateless AND-NOT gate whose one-clock input skew is provided at no cost by SFQ gate-level pipelining. The models are trained directly on the stream representation of the hardware, with a regularizer that bounds the stream gains. Synthesis with an SFQ design flow shows that stochastic streams tolerate relaxed path balancing, which reduces the Josephson-junction (JJ) count of a hard-wired stage by 40-47%.

title: Accelerating MoE Training through Expert Placement and Replica Coordination
summary: Distributed training of sparsely activated mixture-of-experts (MoE) models is often bottlenecked by workload imbalance and all-to-all (A2A) communication induced by dynamic token routing. Existing token deduplication, expert placement, and replication techniques alleviate these bottlenecks but do not jointly capture their distinct load semantics. Under hierarchical token deduplication, communication counts each token once per destination group at each hierarchy level, whereas expert computation processes every token-expert assignment. With replication, both costs depend jointly on physical layout and token-to-copy mapping, making separate optimization suboptimal. We present PlaceMoE to address this coupling. First, we formulate the joint optimization of expert layout and source-aware token-to-copy mapping for E experts distributed across P devices, accounting for both hierarchical communication traffic and expert-compute load. Second, we develop a solver that combines co-selection-aware expert grouping, bounded dynamic programming for replica allocation, and alternating refinement of layout and mapping. Third, PlaceMoE overlaps replica-gradient synchronization with attention backward. We evaluate PlaceMoE on a 32-GPU cluster and a 64-NPU cluster using Qwen3-VL and DeepSeek-V3. Experimental results show that PlaceMoE achieves up to a 6.94x speedup in A2A communication and 1.74-2.33x speedups in end-to-end training over the state-of-the-art training framework VeOmni.

title: Compositional Information Geometry of Probabilistic Programs
summary: We study the compositional, intensional information geometry of probabilistic programs. For a first-order probabilistic programming language with finite random variables, we construct a contravariant lax monoidal functor that, for a program of type $X \to Y$, pulls back a (degenerate) Riemannian metric on $Y$ to $X$. It specialises to the Fisher metric in the case of standard statistical models and to ordinary pullback in the case of deterministic programs. We further justify this construction in two ways. First, we show that this functor arises as a pullback of geometry from a universal space of programs over a type $Y$ with a fixed trace space. Second, we show that it is a special case of a more general pullback construction over weighted measures. Our compositional geometry depends on the presentation of the program, and we study how it relates to the (non-compositional) geometry of the realised measures by establishing a three-level inequality relating our score-velocity metric for the program, the program's corresponding output-conditioned metric, and the standard Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric of the realised family. Finally, we show how the theory can be extended to accommodate continuous random variables using diffeological quasi-Borel spaces. We also discuss several concrete directions for future work.

title: A Fast Greedy Algorithm with a 0.45 Approximation Guarantee for the Airplane Refueling Problem
summary: We study a natural greedy algorithm for the Airplane Refueling Problem (ARP), based on a well-known priority rule. We show that this algorithm achieves an approximation guarantee of $9/20$, noticeably improving the previously known $1/12$ guarantee for a fast algorithm. We also show that the same priority rule can be implemented in $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space using a dynamic convex-hull data structure. These results provide a worst-case approximation guarantee for an existing greedy priority rule and establish an efficient implementation. In the real-RAM model, the running-time bound is independent of the magnitude of the processing times. The resulting method is also suitable as a fast primal routine inside more complex exact and approximation algorithms for large instances. These results narrow the gap between theoretically strong but complex approximation schemes and lightweight algorithms that can be used directly in computational pipelines. The algorithm combines a simple selection rule with a provable performance bound, making it a useful baseline for further algorithmic studies of ARP.

title: Integration, Enhancements and Evaluation of Memory Simulators
summary: Currently, there is no common methodology or set of practices for evaluating memory-system performance in integrated simulation infrastructures. As a result, studies adopt different evaluation approaches, which can lead to conflicting conclusions even for the same simulation infrastructure. We propose a validation methodology that evaluates memory-system performance from three complementary views: the memory simulator, the CPU--memory interface and the simulated application. We use these views to detect, understand and correct memory-simulation inaccuracies arising from simulator integration and simplified modeling of microarchitectural features. The methodology reveals that the application's perception of memory performance can become effectively decoupled from the detailed memory simulation. Most importantly, we identify and correct a fundamental memory-model mismatch between delayed-response cycle-accurate memory simulators and ZSim, a representative parallel CPU simulator. We demonstrate the broader applicability of these enhancements by applying them to ZSim integrations with Ramulator 2, DRAMsim3 and DRAMSys 4, covering all major public cycle-accurate memory simulators. After the corrections and enhancements, all integrations reproduce the main bandwidth--latency trends and key characteristics of the actual system. Across the evaluated simulators, STREAM bandwidth differs from actual-hardware measurements by less than 5% in most experiments, while pointer-chase latency remains 15--18% lower than on actual hardware. All simulator enhancements are released as open source.

title: AgentWeave: Efficient Distributed Agent Serving via Flow Decomposition
summary: Agent applications are evolving into workflows composed of large language model (LLM) calls and tool invocations, termed modules. Existing distributed agent systems typically adopt a disaggregated architecture, deploying different modules on separate devices. While this enables pipeline parallelism, imbalanced module latencies introduce severe pipeline bubbles that limit throughput. A natural alternative is an aggregated architecture that co-deploys all modules across all devices, eliminating bubbles by keeping every device continuously active. However, this introduces request blocking: short requests are forced to progress in lockstep with longer ones in the same batch, and newly arriving requests must wait until the entire ongoing batch completes the full workflow. To address this, we propose AgentWeave, an efficient distributed serving system for agent applications built on the aggregated architecture. Its core mechanism, flow decomposition, decomposes long agent requests into fine-grained execution units while preserving agent semantics, allowing short and newly arriving requests to proceed without being stalled by long-running ones. Complementing this, a flow-adaptive scheduler dynamically balances the throughput gains of decomposition against its scheduling overhead. Experiments across four representative agent applications demonstrate that AgentWeave improves throughput by 1.81x, reduces average latency by 2.45x, and reduces P90 latency by 2.04x over state-of-the-art baselines.

title: OpenMQPI: An MLIR-based Pipeline to Offload Quantum Circuits via OpenMP
summary: Quantum computing introduces specialized software stacks and programming interfaces that are often tightly coupled to specific ecosystems and hardware backends, limiting interoperability and software reuse. For HPCQC application developers, this complicates the integration of quantum accelerators into existing applications. Existing quantum frameworks also use ecosystem-specific circuit representations and compilation pipelines, hindering integration with established heterogeneous compiler infrastructures. We propose OpenMQPI, an MLIR-based OpenMP extension for quantum programming that leverages OpenMP's standardized target offloading infrastructure to integrate quantum resources into HPC applications. OpenMQPI introduces QPIR, a lightweight MLIR dialect for representing quantum circuits within OpenMP target regions, and a compiler pipeline that performs quantum-specific optimizations and lowers circuits to executables compatible with OpenMP offloading. At runtime, an MQSS plugin enables the generated executable to offload quantum circuits to quantum hardware through the OpenMP target offloading model. We evaluate OpenMQPI using the VQE, QFT, and Deutsch-Jozsa algorithms with 5, 10, 15, and 20 qubits, comparing execution times against Qiskit and CUDA Quantum. OpenMQPI achieves the lowest average VQE execution time across all tested qubit configurations. At 20 qubits, it requires 5.18 s, compared with 5.83 s for Qiskit and 7.39 s for CUDA Quantum. For QFT and Deutsch-Jozsa, OpenMQPI achieves execution times comparable to Qiskit and lower than those of CUDA Quantum.

title: Cascade: GPU-Accelerated Out-of-Core Suffix Array Construction for LLM Corpora
summary: Suffix arrays over LLM (pre)training corpora underpin deduplication, contamination testing, n-gram statistics, and training-data attribution, and every new corpus or tokenizer needs a new one. GPU constructors are fast but bounded by device memory, and out-of-core pipelines run at CPU speed, reaching trillions of tokens by building sharded indexes. Reach is bounded not by the size of the data but by what must stay resident, and in a partitioned construction that is the coupling between partitions. We present Cascade, which requires none of it to stay resident. Splitter K-grams sampled from the corpus fix every partition's range of the final suffix array before any sorting, so the GPU sorts and ranks partitions independently and never merges them. The partitions are still coupled: every round of the method needs ranks that other partitions hold, classically kept in a global rank array (the inverse suffix array) that must stay resident. We instead send each rank to the one partition that needs it, and maintain an invariant ensuring ranks are only ever compared within one partition, so no global rank array is needed. The text and a compact partition map, the only structures read at random, then stay in host memory by choice rather than necessity, one at a time when memory is short; every other structure becomes a stream that can be placed across device memory, host memory, and disk as it is written. On a single GPU node, Cascade builds exact suffix arrays of up to 238B tokens, 2.4-6.8x faster than infini-gram's pipeline and 5.9-10.9x faster than libsais.

title: GarageWorks: A Shared Testbench Abstraction for Software Simulation and FPGA Testing
summary: GarageWorks is a lightweight FPGA testing framework that enables the same cocotb testbench to be used for both software RTL simulation and FPGA-accelerated hardware simulation. A shared abstraction hides backend-specific interfaces, while synthesizable Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) dispatchers provide design-under-test (DUT)-specific control and test operations on the FPGA. GarageWorks is intended for rapid bare-metal testing of standalone designs and on-chip processing logic for scientific sensors, rather than full SoC-level prototyping. The framework has been validated on AMD Alveo V80 FPGAs with several internal designs and provides initial support for AI-assisted generation of DUT-specific test components.

title: KedgeFlow: A Programmable Control Plane for Enterprise AI Agents
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Code and artifact available at https://github.com/openkedge/kedgeflow
summary: Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, concurrently reuse the same permission, or retry operations whose responses were lost. These failures arise when approval and resource execution lack a shared contract. KedgeFlow specifies language-independent contracts for trusted controllers to authorize state-changing operations and privileged gateways to enforce that authority independently of agent reasoning. Inspired by OpenFlow, it connects policy checks supported by evidence, signed permission for an exact action, a shared allowance that can be consumed only once, target-side conditions for applying the change, and retained outcome records. Under trusted issuance of exact-action authority, two conditional properties establish at most one successful claim per allowance and link every governed dispatch to a matching grant, claim, and subsequent dispatch authorization, even when the agent is compromised. A reference implementation exposes this execution path to agent systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In the single-resource evaluation, 6,560 concurrent ledger claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances. Boundary tests rejected unauthorized and altered requests before consumption. A 32-call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authorized an undesirable effect, exposing the limits of execution authorization. Evaluation uses three members of the etcd coordinated key-value store on one host, synthetic authentication and authorization inputs, and a mock target that rejects stale requests. Distributed reservations, enforcement of every production access route, native crash recovery, exactly-once effects at real targets, and interoperability between independent implementations remain untested.

title: Solving Restricted Versions of #SAT Faster than $2^m$: Algorithms and Lower Bounds
summary:
Under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$, the #SAT problem (counting the number of satisfying assignments of a CNF formula) cannot be solved in $\mathcal{O}^*((2-\varepsilon)^n)$ or $\mathcal{O}^*((2-\varepsilon)^m)$ time, where $n$ is the number of variables and $m$ is the number of clauses. On the other hand, simple exhaustive search and the standard inclusion-exclusion give $\mathcal{O}^*(2^n)$-time and $\mathcal{O}^*(2^m)$-time algorithms, respectively. A natural line of research is to beat these SETH-based barriers for restricted versions, such as #$k$-SAT (where each clause contains at most $k$ literals) or #$d$-occ-SAT (where each variable appears in at most $d$ clauses). It is known that the $2^n$-barrier can be broken when $k$ or $d$ is any constant; yet, whether the $2^m$-barrier can also be broken in these cases remains unknown.
  We present two simple algorithms that overcome the $2^m$-barrier. First, for #$k$-SAT, we give an $\mathcal{O}^*(2^{m(1-1/O(k))})$-time algorithm, thereby breaking the $2^m$-barrier for any constant $k$. Second, for #$2$-occ-SAT (which also includes the problem of counting the number of edge covers in a graph as a special case), we provide an algorithm with runtime $\mathcal{O}^*(2^{mω/3})$, where $ω< 2.3714$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both algorithms generalize to the weighted counting setting while preserving the same runtime bounds.
  On the hardness side, we present a reduction from #Max-$d$-SAT to #$d$-occ-SAT, showing that for any $d\ge 3$, #$d$-occ-SAT admits no $\mathcal{O}^*((2-\varepsilon)^m)$-time algorithm for any constant $\varepsilon>0$, even on positive formulas, under the hypothesis that #Max-3-SAT on $n$ variables admits no $\mathcal{O}^*((2-\varepsilon)^n)$-time algorithm for any such $\varepsilon$.

title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays
summary: Systolic arrays are widely used to accelerate neural-network inference, yet fixed two-dimensional arrays struggle with the substantial diversity in both matrix geometry and available parallelism across CNNs and Transformer-based large language models. This mismatch is particularly severe for skinny matrices, small-batch autoregressive decoding, and operators containing multiple independent partitions, leading to low processing-element (PE) utilization and repeated spatial folding. Existing reconfigurable arrays typically improve either shape adaptation or distributed execution, whereas supporting both through fine-grained routing incurs considerable interconnect, buffering, and control overheads. We present LizTail (named after lizard tail autotomy, where predefined fracture planes allow segments to detach and remain independently active, analogous to LizTail's predefined reconfiguration boundaries), a multi-mode systolic array that enables constrained segment-level reconfiguration by partitioning a $128\times128$ array into 32 regular $128\times4$ segments and adding connectivity only at predefined endpoints. The resulting substrate supports trimming, long-path extension through $180^\circ$ turn-back connections, and distributed execution in which each subarray can itself be trimmed or extended. Differentiated PE datapaths and segment-aware CEB/SIB buffers provide the required compute and data-delivery flexibility without unrestricted PE-level routing. A hardware-constrained mapper selects the execution organization, dataflow, task partition, and tiling. Across representative workloads, LizTail achieves geometric-mean speedups of $5.02\times$ on CNN inference and $25.67\times$ on LLM decoding over a TPU-like array, while reducing EDP by up to $38.23\times$. LizTail is open-sourced at https://github.com/kmjbwxa/LizTail.

title: Seamless Deployment of Machine Learning Inference at the Far Edge: An Empirical AWS IoT Greengrass Architecture for Industrial Predictive Maintenance
comment: Conference paper draft in IEEE format, with code appendices. Already accepted in AiBThings - IEEE 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain and Internet of Things
summary: Industrial IoT sensors produce continuous, high-volume data streams that predictive maintenance needs to analyse in real time. Cloud-centric architectures send all raw telemetry to central servers, which costs latency, bandwidth and resilience. This paper presents a hybrid cloud-edge architecture for manufacturing predictive maintenance built on AWS IoT Core and AWS IoT Greengrass v2, with local machine learning inference at the edge and selective cloud synchronization. We deploy two configurations on real AWS infrastructure and compare them: a cloud-only baseline (Configuration A) and the proposed hybrid edge architecture (Configuration B). We measure end-to-end inference latency, bandwidth consumption and inference accuracy. Configuration B cuts cloud-bound bandwidth by 86.8% (63.6 KB to 7.2 KB per 200-reading window) and decision latency by 256x (23.1 ms cloud round trip to 0.09 ms local inference). At the edge, with no cloud involvement, it keeps an anomaly-class F1 score of 0.84 and 91% recall. The evaluation also instruments system uptime and Stream Manager queuing under cloud disconnection; the quantitative disconnection experiment is left as planned work. Our review of the literature points to four gaps that this work addresses: the lack of empirically validated Greengrass v2 deployments for predictive maintenance, unquantified bandwidth savings from selective edge synchronization, unmeasured resilience under cloud disconnection, and the open MLOps feedback loop at the edge.

title: Optimal High Probability Bounds for Random Order Online Sorting
summary: In random order online sorting, a fixed multiset of $n$ real numbers arrives in a uniformly random order. Each value must be placed immediately and irrevocably into an empty position of an array with exactly $n$ positions. The objective is to minimize the sum of the absolute differences between consecutive entries. If the entire input were known in advance, sorting the values would be optimal and would have cost equal to the range of the input. We prove that the optimal worst case competitive ratio in this model is $Θ(\log n)$ with high probability. In particular, we give a single online algorithm that achieves an $O(\log n)$ competitive ratio with high probability for every fixed input, and we show that every randomized online algorithm has some fixed input on which an $Ω(\log n)$ ratio is unavoidable with high probability. The same upper bound also holds for independent samples from an arbitrary unknown distribution on the real line. The algorithm uses the random arrival order to learn the relative positions of future values from the values seen so far. It maintains a hierarchy of small regions of the input order and allows an arriving value to use nearby space when its preferred region is full. This flexibility avoids the need to reserve large amounts of space for unlikely local fluctuations. The analysis shows that large displacements become rapidly less likely as their scale grows, leading to the $O(\log n)$ high probability bound. A matching lower bound shows that no randomized online algorithm can improve the logarithmic dependence in the worst case.

title: SafeDSE: Joint Exploration of Safety Architecture Patterns, Mapping, and Scheduling for Dataflow Applications With Safety Arguments (Extended Version)
comment: 38 pages, 12 figures, 29 tables. Extended version of a paper submitted for publication; tool and data at github.com/SBU-CPS-Lab/SafeDSE
summary: Embedded platforms increasingly host safety-related streaming functions next to less critical ones. Whether a safety architecture pattern, such as a doer/checker pair, protects a function depends on the cores that run its components. Their schedule must meet the throughput requirement, and mixing safety integrity levels (SILs) on one core raises development cost. This report presents SafeDSE, a design space exploration framework for synchronous dataflow applications. One declarative constraint model decides the pattern of each actor, the placement that the fault model requires, the static-order schedule, and the platform, and prices SIL promotion. Guards activate the chosen patterns in a fixed graph that holds all of them, and node potentials encode throughput. An independent verifier re-checks every solution, and a generator turns its checks into evidence of a safety argument in Goal Structuring Notation. On 9 benchmark instances under period bounds, no rule that fixes patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive under conservative pricing, while joint exploration was. In the generated arguments, 49 to 62% of the leaves cite verifier checks; the rest are claims a mapping cannot discharge. Optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs with up to 16 actors. This extended version adds the full model, the verifier and generator in detail, the complete catalog and parameters, and a proof of the potential characterization. It also reports every experiment per instance, a mutation analysis of the verifier, and the negative results of the development.

title: Weighted Beeping Networks
summary: Beeping Networks (BN) have become an established model of wireless communication and computation. They assume, however, that the communication interference caused by beeping nodes is binary (OR channel), while both artificial and nature-driven networks are based on varied signal strength and receiving thresholds. This work naturally extends the classic beeping networks to weighted beeping networks (WBN), by modeling signal strengths by weights on graph edges and receiving a beep if the accumulative signal strengths of transmitting neighbors are above receiving threshold. Under this generalized model, we study the fundamental Local Broadcast (LB) problem. Since edges with low weights may not even accumulate to a received beep, we only require that messages are delivered along sufficiently heavy edges, with weights above some given threshold $σ$. We design an LB algorithm that completes its task in $O(I_σ\log n \cdot (\mathcal{M}+\log n))$ beeping rounds, whp, where $n$ is the number of nodes, $I_σ$ is the maximum local interference on heavy edges, and $\mathcal{M}$ is the maximum length of messages sent locally. This result is nearly optimal, as, with probability $1$, $Ω(I_σ)$ beeping rounds are necessary to solve LB. Finally, we show that any algorithm designed for the classic beeping networks and terminating in polynomial number of beeping rounds, can be emulated on any WBN with a logarithmic overhead, that is, it returns the same output as working on the classic beeping network isomorphic to the sub-graph of heavy edges.

title: FirstFit coloring process of random bipartite graphs and an online coloring lower bound in the random order model
summary: FirstFit colors each arriving vertex with the smallest positive integer absent from its previously colored neighborhood. We prove that this rule can require $n^{Ω(1)}$ many colors on certain bipartite graph of $n$ vertices even when the vertices arrive in a uniformly random order. This refutes the conjecture of Bosek, Gutowski, Lasoń, and Przybyło [BGLP24] that FirstFit uses a polylogarithmic expected number of colors on every bipartite graph in the random order model. We obtain the lower bound by analyzing the FirstFit coloring process on random bipartite graphs, where vertices arrive to either side with equal probability, and with an independent edge density $n^{-x}$ for some $0 < x < 1$. Our result can also be viewed as a qualitative strengthening of Kučera [Kuč91], who showed that, for every $ε> 0$, there are graphs with chromatic number at most $n^ε$ on which FirstFit uses $Ω(n/\log n)$ colors in expectation under a uniformly random order. Our result shows that such poor behavior of FirstFit already occurs for $χ(G) = 2$.

title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
summary: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).

title: DualColl: Throughput-Optimal Bandwidth-Bound Collective Communications via Fractional Tree Packing
summary:
Large-scale distributed training increasingly makes collective communication bandwidth-bound. In modern GPU clusters, communication libraries such as NCCL implement collectives including AllReduce over heterogeneous interconnects such as NVLink, InfiniBand, and Ethernet, making efficient use of available network bandwidth a central systems challenge.
  ForestColl showed that collective communication on such fabrics can be formulated using fractional tree packing; its scalable polynomial-time construction is developed for AllGather, with AllReduce obtained by composing AllGather and ReduceScatter. We present DualColl, which targets bandwidth-bound AllReduce directly. Under the tree-based AllReduce model, DualColl applies a Garg--Könemann-style multiplicative-weights algorithm and, for any $0<ε<1$, computes a feasible schedule whose throughput is at least $(1-ε)^2$ of the optimal AllReduce throughput. Its key component is an exact minimum-cost collective-tree oracle that projects physical-link dual prices onto a logical graph of participating ranks, reducing each iteration to shortest-path computations followed by a minimum spanning tree.
  We further extend the framework to local equal-next-hop packet-sprayed routing and to networks without explicit per-tree bandwidth control. For the latter, we introduce a tree-coupled max-min bandwidth-sharing model and show that tree duplication approximates an explicit fractional allocation with a provable accuracy-complexity tradeoff. Finally, we extend the fractional-packing framework to additional collective operations and multiple concurrent collective groups.

title: Approximation Algorithms for Dual-Memory Request Scheduling in Disaggregated LLM Inference
summary: Disaggregated LLM inference executes the prefill and decode phases on separate resource pools, reducing interference between the two phases. However, this architecture introduces a coupled scheduling problem because a request that completes prefill retains its prompt KV cache in prefill memory until it is admitted to the decode pool. Prefill and decode admission decisions therefore jointly determine memory occupancy and request completion times. To the best of our knowledge, this problem lacks a formal formulation, and no approximation guarantees are known for request scheduling in disaggregated LLM inference. We formalize this setting as the dual-memory request scheduling (DMRS) problem, whose objective is to minimize the sum of request completion times, and prove that it is strongly NP-hard. We develop two deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithms. The first applies to instances satisfying $α<1$ and $β<1$ and achieves an approximation ratio of $8+\frac{4}{1-α}+\frac{8}{1-β}$, where $α$ and $β$ are the maximum normalized prefill and peak decode memory demands among all requests, respectively. In particular, it yields a $32$-approximation when $α,β\leq 1/2$. The second algorithm applies to all feasible instances and achieves a uniform $36$-approximation. Finally, evaluations on two H100 GPUs using trace-derived offline workloads show that the proposed algorithms reduce the sum of request completion times relative to multiple vLLM deployment baselines.

title: LocalTrain: Integer-Only Local Learning for Energy-Efficient CNN Training on Edge FPGAs
summary: Local learning reduces cross-layer training dependencies, but an efficient accelerator must still retain operands, accumulate gradients, and select quantization scales. We present an FPGA system that trains a CNN and its regional auxiliary classifiers using a shared integer matrix engine. Compact errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales permit direct output conversion. At 200 MHz, the KV260 prototype achieves 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at approximately 4.20 W mean module power. Effective matrix throughput is 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s, respectively. Against the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, measured training energy is 40.4% and 42.1% lower, with $1.86\times$ and $1.82\times$ longer runtime; measurements use the respective platform power domains. Selected state checks and matching complete-run prediction counts support functional agreement with the software reference.

title: Native Dual Pools or Shared Paging? Memory Organization for Concurrent Hybrid LLM Serving
comment: 10 pages of main text, 31 pages of supplementary appendices. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems
summary: Hybrid attention-SSM serving combines growing attention KV with fixed-size recurrent and convolution state whose allocation units, reuse boundaries, and lifetimes differ. We implement four memory organizations in a modified vLLM runtime: a coarse shared-page baseline (S0), checkpoint-internal recurrent paging (S1), paging with convolution-slot packing (S2), and native dual pools (D0). Nine evaluation questions cover storage costs and serving behavior. The cumulative S0-S1-S2 refinement improves completed-output throughput and tail completion time at the main operating point. D0-S2 performance varies with memory budget, offered load, and admission headroom. Shared-prefix workloads yield larger stepwise gains; gains also persist in a no-sharing control with equal recorded input-work totals. State traces identify recurrent-checkpoint availability as the limit on joint reuse in the tested S2 runs. Extending producer-side checkpoint lifetime increases reusable depth at a fixed page budget. A fresh-seed SHARE/ISOLATE comparison estimates a positive retention interaction, with a primary confidence interval that includes zero. Retained-state continuation correctness remains unresolved. These findings motivate evaluating physical state representation together with request admission and checkpoint lifetime when designing memory management for concurrent hybrid-model serving.

title: Almost Lossless Transfer for Cuttable Distributed Problems
summary: We study constant-round LOCAL approximation for additive local vertex-subset minimization problems. Given a $k$-uniform $α$-approximation on a hereditary source class closed under disjoint union, Bonamy, Das, Gavoille, Picavet, Suomela, and Wesolek obtained ratio $α(d+1)+1$ on locally nice target classes of asymptotic dimension $d$. We prove two transfers with ratios $α+1+η$ and $α+η$ for every $η>0$. These bounds require the stronger local niceness assumption at a larger scale that depends on $η$. The first algorithm keeps their repair construction and increases the radius used to detect errors. We average over partitions of the graph to bound the retained cost without the factor $d+1$. These partitions are used only in the analysis. The second algorithm tests several deletion widths around the errors. In each component of the repair zone, it chooses a smallest union of retained choices and an exact repair. Averaging over the widths bounds the cost counted twice and yields ratio $α+η$. Both transfers are deterministic and computable, use arbitrary distinct numerical identifiers, and need no knowledge of the graph size. Their outputs also satisfy local uniformity guarantees. For 2-domination on graphs of bounded Euler genus, the same planar source gives ratio $19$ through the earlier transfer and $6+η$ through ours. For minimum dominating set, our transfer gives ratio $7+\varepsilon$ on graphs formed by attaching a clique of arbitrary size at one vertex of a planar graph, using the source algorithm of Amiri and Siebertz. This class satisfies our target assumptions and allows nonempty error sets. Its Euler genus is unbounded, so their guarantee for graphs of bounded Euler genus does not cover the whole class.

title: When Is RTL Better? Auditing Evaluation Stability with Tool-Grounded Requirement Profiles
summary: RTL-generation studies increasingly report functional correctness and post-synthesis quality, yet the evaluator itself is rarely treated as an experimental variable. A candidate can appear better when a security rule, protocol obligation, target context, feasibility gate, uncertainty policy, or provenance constraint is omitted. We introduce tool-grounded requirement profiles: machine-readable contracts binding each requirement's meaning to its executable evidence and comparison rule, together with cross-requirement gates, uncertainty handling, and provenance. We audit evaluator stability by freezing candidate pairs and perturbing only their evaluation profile. In a preregistered controlled pilot with six designs, twelve pairs, three requirement families, six evaluator conditions, and 72 decisions, a generic cell-count evaluator reports unsupported improvement for 6/12 pairs (50%; Wilson 95% interval 25.4 to 74.6%; design-cluster bootstrap interval 25 to 75%). The matched evaluator detects all twelve injected regressions, whereas syntax, generic synthesis, context mismatch, and gate ablation each lose the required distinction for 12/12 pairs. In a separately frozen external validation of all 290 public RTLLM v1.1 text-only candidates, 81/215 evaluable comparisons (37.7%; task-cluster 95% interval 24.8 to 51.4%) yield unsupported scalar improvements, including 72 functional-gate reversals. Separately, 26 OpenROAD-flow-scripts runs show why timing context and activity qualification must be part of the contract. The study does not rank generators; it establishes evaluator configuration as a measurable, auditable source of conclusion instability.

title: Multi-GPU Communication Schemes for Iterative Solvers: When CPUs are Not in Charge
summary: This paper proposes a fully autonomous execution model for multi-GPU applications that completely excludes the involvement of the CPU beyond the initial kernel launch. In a typical multi-GPU application, the host serves as the orchestrator of execution by directly launching kernels, issuing communication calls, and acting as a synchronizer for devices. We argue that this orchestration, or control flow path, causes undue overhead and can be delegated entirely to devices to improve performance in applications that require communication among peers. For the proposed CPU-free execution model, we leverage existing techniques such as persistent kernels, thread block specialization, device-side barriers, and device-initiated communication routines to write fully autonomous multi-GPU code and achieve significantly reduced communication overheads. We demonstrate our proposed model on two broadly used iterative solvers, 2D/3D Jacobi stencil and Conjugate Gradient(CG). Compared to the CPU-controlled baselines, the CPU-free model can improve 3D stencil communication latency by 58.8% and provide a 1.63x speedup for CG on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The project code is available at https://github.com/ParCoreLab/CPU-Free-model.

title: Metric Planarity Testing is Hard
summary:
A key milestone in algorithmic graph theory is Hopcroft and Tarjan's 1974 linear-time algorithm for graph planarity testing. At a workshop in 2002, Linial and Rabinovich asked for either a polynomial-time algorithm or an NP-hardness proof for metric planarity testing: given a metric space $(X,d_X)$, determine whether there exists an edge-weighted planar graph $G=(V,E,w)$ with $X\subseteq V$ that realizes the distances in $X$, meaning that $d_G(x,y)=d_X(x,y)$ for every $x,y\in X$. This question arose in the context of research on metric embeddings and their applications in computer science since the mid-1990s. Over the past few decades, polynomial-time algorithms have been developed for several special cases.
  In this work, we show that metric planarity testing is NP-hard, in sharp contrast to graph planarity testing. Our reduction yields a stronger result: under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), no $2^{o(n)}$-time algorithm for metric planarity testing exists, where $n$ is the number of points in the metric.
  To complement our ETH lower bound, we give two algorithmic results: (i) an algorithm for computing a metric planar embedding in $2^{\tilde{O}(n^2)}$ time and (ii) a $(1+ε)$-approximation algorithm in $2^{\tilde{O}(n)}$ time for any fixed $ε\in(0,1)$. The second algorithm produces a planar graph that preserves the input metric up to a factor of $(1+ε)$.

title: Formal-Verification-Guided Bayesian Optimization for Non-Intrusive Last-Mile Coverage Closure
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Accepted for publication in ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems (TODAES)
summary: Last-mile functional coverage closure for modern chip designs remains costly because a mature UVM environment exposes many controls while direct hits on the remaining bins are sparse. We present a non-intrusive workflow that closes pre-defined bins in an existing, human-authored functional coverage model; it does not synthesize verification objectives from the design specification. The workflow first uses abstract-syntax-tree (AST) parsing and cone-of-influence (COI) tracing to map each residual target to existing testbench knobs. Under a matched 20-simulation budget, Bayesian optimization (BO) is compared with continued constrained-random verification (CRV) and random search over the same AST/COI-reduced space. Formal reachability then removes only targets supported by complete unreachability proofs, after which retained targets are grouped by formal difficulty and processed by group-specific BO under a second matched 20-simulation budget. Cleanup and grouping never add numerator bins; only simulator coverage artifacts do. On OpenTitan AES, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 241/271 bins; formal cleanup removes two denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 20 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 261/271 raw coverage (96.31%) and 261/269 effective coverage (97.03%). On Entropy Source, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 2117/2277 bins; formal cleanup removes ten denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 93 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 2210/2277 raw coverage (97.06%) and 2210/2267 effective coverage (97.49%). These results characterize the integrated diagnosis-and-search workflow; the present evaluation does not isolate the causal contributions of difficulty classification, policy routing, and post-cleanup BO.

title: Learning based Scalable Multi-Objective Scheduling of Workflows across UD-IaaS-FaaS Systems
